newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Air cargo market to pick up in 1997 -Lehman Bros.
newsitem.headline: Air cargo market to pick up in 1997 -Lehman Bros.

text.p: U.S. investment bank Lehman Brothers said the air cargo market was showing signs of stabilising and demand increasing somewhat, reversing a weak 12 month period, according to a report received on Friday.
Capacity was also increasing at a slower rate than before, the bank said in its market research called European Airlines & Airports and dated November 14.

"At the time of writing, the cargo market is showing some signs of stabilisation with demand showing slightly stronger growth and, most importantly, capacity growth back down to low single digit growth rates."
Cargo rates may even be on the rise, Lehman Brothers said.
"Cargo load factors appear to have turned the corner and the impact should feed through to price stabilisation and maybe even price increases."
Next year would be a better year for cargo operations, but European airlines were unlikely to benefit from cargo because of the sector's low yields, it said.

"In 1997 we would expect a better performance from the cargo sector, but it remains a low yield product being produced in a high cost environment, and as such we would not expect it ever to be seen as a major profit contributor for any European flag carrier."

It said lower GDP growth in Europe, in Germany in particular, was behind the slowdown in demand which fell from 15 to 20 percent for several airlines in the past two years to nearer five percent in 1996.
An increase in freight capacity had eroded prices and airlines such as KLM Royal Dutch Airlines NV and Deutsche Lufthansa AG, would be hit, it said.
"Aggregate increases in capacity have outstripped increases in demand, to the entent that cargo load factors have fallen and pricing has been severely eroded."

"Specifically in Europe, KLM and Lufthansa of the commercialised airlines have a substantial exposure to the cargo market, in both cases accounting for around 45 percent of total traffic and 20 percent of total revenues."
It said British Airways and Swissair would be less affected by the weak 1996 market.
"These airlines do not have dedicated cargo aircraft, and only have exposure to the cargo business as an inescapable by-product of their core passenger business."
